fields.short: These studies can't say if it's the truth. But after a retreat, beliefs shifted a bit, towards ideas like other worlds and a conscious universe. The shift was still there 6 months later.
fields.but: The main study had no comparison group, and only 122 of over 800 people answered every survey. Most already leaned that way.
how: People answered questions a week before a psychedelic retreat or ceremony, then 4 weeks and 6 months after. In the 122 who answered all three, belief in things like other worlds rose a little.
First-timers shifted more. In one exploratory analysis, the shift went with feeling in tune with the group, not clearly with how mystical or visual the trip felt.
In a trial in depression, beliefs shifted after psilocybin. They shifted a little after a standard antidepressant too, and the gap was too small to be sure of.

A survey asked 1,606 people who said a trip had changed their beliefs to look back, about 8 years on average. 26 in 100 recalled thinking plants could be conscious before, and 61 in 100 after. Superstitions, like black cats bringing bad luck, didn't rise.

how: People see simple shapes after LSD or cannabis. They also come with flickering light or when falling asleep. An earlier researcher sorted these into four types: lattices and honeycombs, cobwebs, tunnels, and spirals.
The wiring from eye to brain turns a tunnel or a spiral into plain stripes. These run across the brain's first area for sight.
In the model, when that area gets too excitable, stripes and lattices of activity form by themselves, shaped by how its cells connect. Mapped back to what you'd see, they look like all four types.
The wiring data came mostly from cats and monkeys. The best matches needed wider connections than that anatomy shows, and some complex visions don't fit the model.

how: 12 healthy adults who had used MDA, or MDMA and LSD-type drugs, took MDA and a dummy pill in hospital, not told which. Their results were set beside earlier MDMA results from other people.
MDA was rated higher than MDMA for visions and 'spiritual' feelings, and lower for anxiety and loss of control. Both made people feel close to others.
Heart rate rose about 20 beats a minute after MDA and 31 after MDMA, though the paper calls them similar. Top blood pressure rose about 30 points with both.
The paper calls MDA well tolerated, but doesn't report the side effects it checked for. Why MDMA is more popular wasn't studied.

fields.short: People say desire often goes up, erections can go either way, and orgasm often takes longer. In one survey, 8 of 20 men said erections got weaker on MDMA, and 8 stronger.
how: In Israel, 20 men and 15 women who had used MDMA before sex compared it, from memory, with their usual sex. All 35 said desire went up, and 32 said they were more satisfied.
Of the 20 men, 8 said erections got weaker and 8 stronger. 16 of 20 men and 6 of 15 women said orgasm took longer, and 3 people said they couldn't reach it but were still more satisfied.
In Northern Ireland, 98 people were interviewed. A little over half said MDMA was more about closeness than sex. Some men said they couldn't get an erection; others described strong desire.
Some described one-night stands and regret. Condoms were rare on ecstasy, but also rare without drugs, so the study can't show MDMA made sex riskier.

fields.short: People felt just as drunk as on alcohol alone, but less sleepy, and test scores fell about as far. Blood MDMA peaked 13% higher, in a lab study of 9 men.
how: 9 healthy men who had taken MDMA before each had four lab sessions, a week apart. They got MDMA, alcohol, both, or neither, with dummy pills and drinks so they wouldn't know which.
With both, the sleepy feeling from alcohol went away. Feeling drunk didn't: if anything, it was rated a bit higher, though not clearly.
On a timed symbol test, scores at their worst fell about as much as with alcohol alone, but for about 1 hour, not 2 to 3. Only with both was reaction time clearly slower than with the dummy.

Blood MDMA peaked 13% higher and blood alcohol 15% lower; the authors call these small changes. Nobody rated how well they thought they did, though they felt more energetic and efficient than with alcohol alone. Nobody drove.

fields.but: These are police and death records, which can't show what share of street pills hold fentanyl. Death records likely miss many fake pills.
how: US police records: of seizures that held fentanyl, pills were 14 in 100 in early 2018 and 29 in 100 in late 2021. The rest were powder. Fentanyl pills seized in three months rose from about 42,000 to about 2.1 million.

Death records from 29 states and Washington, DC: deaths with signs of fake pills went from 2 in 100 in mid-2019 to a high of about 5 in 100 in mid-2021, then stayed near there. In western states, about 5 became about 15 in 100.

In 2021, 55 in 100 of these deaths involved fake oxycodone only, often marked 'M-30', and 17 in 100 fake alprazolam (Xanax) only. Fentanyl or similar drugs were among the recorded causes in 93 in 100.
Neither record shows how much fentanyl the pills held or what else was in them, and death records don't say how many pills were tested. A drug-checking study in Vancouver tested too few pills to say.

how: The idea: the place, the people and the ritual that come with a drug start to trigger the body's push-back against it. That push-back is part of tolerance, so it may be weaker somewhere new.
In rat studies from the same researcher, tolerance was weaker in a new place, and a large dose of heroin was more often deadly there. Rats aren't people.
Of 10 overdose survivors, 7 recalled something unusual that day: 3 a new place or crowd, 2 a different way of injecting, 2 a different mix of drugs. The other 3 recalled nothing unusual.
Nobody counted how often people use somewhere new without an overdose. A later review by the same researcher suggests a treatment based on the idea, but cites no test of it.

fields.short: Deaths were more common off treatment, most of all in the first 4 weeks after leaving. In 16 methadone studies, about 36 in 1,000 died a year off treatment, against 11 on it.
how: In 16 groups of people on methadone, about 11 in 1,000 died each year in treatment, against about 36 out of it. Every group had more deaths out of treatment.
In the biggest recent groups the gap was smaller: about 6 or 7 deaths a year per 1,000 people in treatment, against 12 to 18 out of it.
Deaths in the first 4 weeks off methadone ran at about 32 a year per 1,000 people, against about 14 later on. The first month on methadone looked riskier too, but that could be chance.

In the 3 groups that split overdose deaths by time, they weren't clearly higher in the first 4 weeks after leaving than later. Buprenorphine looked similar, but from just three groups, mostly one Australian study.
